title: Implementation Strategy

title: Task 2 - Output All Pairs Problem Statement
summary: Introduces Task 2: outputting all possible unordered pairs (a,b) from array values, asking whether this can be done in a single pass.
main_text: Task 2. Output all possible pairs of numbers (a,b). Order does NOT matter [Don't output (b,a) after outputting (a,b)]. Questions: How many pairs are there? How many (4,x) pairs? title: Task 2 - Programming Mechanics

title: Task 3 - Uniqueness with Large Data
summary: Shows that checking uniqueness becomes harder for humans with larger datasets, motivating the need for a systematic algorithmic approach.
main_text: Task 3. Check if all the numbers in an array are unique. It may not be as easy even for a human when we increase the amount of numbers? Questions: What process would you use as a human? Can we do this in 1 pass? If we can only see 1 thing or perform 1 operation at a time, what other variables do we need? Do we always have to do the same amount of work, or might we find an answer 'early'? Sample Data: 6 40 3 96 44 94 74 9 23 22 56 64 12 7 51 31 24 80 88 10 91 27 38 30 78 60 37 69 26 11 39 50 68 21 41 48 66 46 20 25 82 98 76 34 55 70 4 54 90 28 14 71 73 85 81 65 77 59 57 43 33 49 87 19 17 16 1 2 15 72 45 93 86 92 36
notes_text: With ~75 numbers, manual uniqueness checking is impractical. This reinforces why we need a nested loop algorithm.

images.description: A box containing 75 sample numbers arranged in rows, demonstrating the difficulty of visually checking uniqueness in a large dataset.

title: Task 3 - Uniqueness Check Trace (First Element)
summary: Traces comparing element at index 0 (value 5) against all subsequent elements using indices J=0 and K=1 through 6.
main_text: Task 3. Check if all numbers are unique. The trace shows comparing the first element (5) against all others: J=0, K=1: compare data[0]=5 with data[1]=2. J=0, K=2: compare 5 with data[2]=8. J=0, K=3: compare 5 with data[3]=1. J=0, K=4: compare 5 with data[4]=7. J=0, K=5: compare 5 with data[5]=9. J=0, K=6: compare 5 with data[6]=3. We've seen all the numbers now? Can we state they are all unique? What are you 'remembering' to answer that question? Can the computer do that?
notes_text: After comparing element 0 against all others, we only know that 5 has no duplicate - we still need to check all other pairs.

images.description: Six array state diagrams showing J=0 fixed while K increments from 1 to 6, each highlighting the two elements being compared from the array [5,2,8,1,7,9,3].

title: Task 3 - Why K Should Not Start at 0
summary: Explains why the inner loop index K must not start at 0 to avoid comparing an element with itself, which would always yield a false duplicate.
main_text: Task 3. Why not start k at 0 as well? We never want to compare an element with itself. The diagram shows J=0, K=0 with a prohibition symbol, and the comparison data[j] == data[k] would be data[0] == data[0], which is always true and would incorrectly indicate a duplicate.
notes_text: This is a common mistake when implementing the uniqueness check. Starting K at J+1 avoids self-comparison and also avoids redundant pair checks.

images.description: Array diagram with J=0, K=0 both pointing to the same element, with a red prohibition/no symbol indicating this is wrong. A box shows data[j] == data[k] to illustrate the self-comparison problem.

title: Task 3 - Uniqueness Check Trace (Second Element)
summary: Continues the uniqueness trace with J=1, comparing element at index 1 (value 2) against elements at indices 2 through 6.
main_text: Task 3. Check if all numbers are unique. Trace continues with J=1: J=1, K=2: compare data[1]=2 with data[2]=8. J=1, K=3: compare 2 with data[3]=1. J=1, K=4: compare 2 with data[4]=7. J=1, K=5: compare 2 with data[5]=9. J=1, K=6: compare 2 with data[6]=3. No duplicates found for element at index 1.
notes_text: The pattern continues: for each J, K starts at J+1 and goes to the end. This ensures each pair is checked exactly once.

images.description: Five array state diagrams showing J=1 fixed while K goes from 2 to 6, highlighting the two compared elements each time.

title: Task 3 - Final Pair in Uniqueness Check
summary: Shows the last comparison in the uniqueness check with J=5, K=6 comparing the final pair of elements.
main_text: Task 3. Check if all numbers are unique. Final comparison: J=5, K=6: compare data[5]=9 with data[6]=3. These are the last two elements to compare, completing all pairwise checks.
notes_text: This shows the end of the nested loop execution. All pairs have been checked with no duplicates found.

images.description: Single array state diagram showing J=5, K=6 as the final pair comparison.

title: Task 3 - Uniqueness Programming Mechanics
summary: Presents the key programming questions for implementing the uniqueness check: index dependency, output timing, and stopping conditions.
main_text: Task 3. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Are the indexes independent or is one dependent on another? How and when are we ready to print our answer? How do we stop (one or both loops)? Code template: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task ... return 0; }
notes_text: Key decisions: use a bool flag (allUnique), break out of inner loop when duplicate found, break out of outer loop too. Answer is printed after both loops complete or after early termination.

title: Task 4 - Reverse Array Problem Statement
summary: Introduces Task 4: reversing an array of integers, questioning whether it needs a nested loop or can be done in one pass.
main_text: Task 4. Reverse an array of integers. Question: Can we do this in 1 pass or do we need a nested loop where we examine 'pairs'? Example: Reverse an array's contents. Before: data = [4, 8, -3, 12, -5, 6, 17, -10, 9] at indices [0] through [8]. After: data = [9, -10, 17, 6, -5, 12, -3, 8, 4]. A red downward arrow indicates the transformation from original to reversed array.
notes_text: This task can be done in a single pass with two pointers moving toward each other, not requiring nested loops.

images.description: Two array diagrams showing the before and after states of reversing the array, connected by a red downward arrow.

title: Task 4 - Array Reversal Trace (Swapping)
summary: Traces the array reversal process showing swaps between elements at positions J and K moving inward from both ends.
main_text: Task 4. Reverse an array's contents. Trace with J (left pointer) and K (right pointer) and n=9: J=0, K=8: swap data[0]=4 with data[8]=9. J=1, K=7: swap data[1]=8 with data[7]=-10. J=2, K=6: swap data[2]=-3 with data[6]=17. J=3, K=5: swap data[3]=12 with data[5]=6. J=4, K=4: J meets K at the middle element -5. A question mark indicates: should we keep going? Pink double-headed arrows show each swap operation.
notes_text: When J equals K (or J > K), we have reached the middle and should stop. The middle element does not need to be swapped.

images.description: Five array state diagrams showing the progressive swapping from both ends toward the middle, with pink double-headed arrows indicating each swap. Variables J, K, and n are tracked on the right.

title: Task 4 - Why Stop at Halfway
summary: Demonstrates that continuing swaps past the halfway point undoes the reversal, so the loop must stop at n/2.
main_text: Task 4. Should we keep going? The trace continues past the middle showing what happens if we don't stop: J=2, K=6: swap -3 and 17 (correct). J=3, K=5: swap 12 and 6 (correct). J=4, K=4: middle element -5 (stop here). J=5, K=3: swap 6 and 12 - this UNDOES the earlier swap! J=6, K=2: swap 17 and -3 - this UNDOES another earlier swap! No! We must stop at the halfway point to avoid 'undoing' the swaps we've just done.
notes_text: This is a crucial insight: the loop condition must be j < n/2 (or equivalently j < k). Going past the middle reverses the reversal.

images.description: Array state diagrams showing swaps continuing past the midpoint, with the last two swaps undoing previous work. A warning box at the bottom explains why stopping at halfway is necessary.

title: Task 4 - Reversal Programming Mechanics
summary: Discusses implementation considerations for array reversal including even/odd length handling and index dependency.
main_text: Task 4. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Does an even or odd length array need to be handled separately? Can we do this in 1 pass or do we need a nested loop where we examine 'pairs'? Are the indexes we need to generate independent or is one dependent on another? Code template: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task ... return 0; }
notes_text: Even and odd length arrays are handled the same way with j < n/2. For odd arrays, the middle element stays in place. The two indexes are dependent: k = n-1-j.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted C++ code template for array setup.

title: Task 5 - Move Negatives to Front
summary: Introduces Task 5: moving all negative numbers to the front of an array while preserving the order of negative numbers.
main_text: Task 5. Move all negative numbers to the front of the array, preserving order of negative numbers (but not necessarily positive numbers). Question: Can we do this in 1 pass or do we need a nested loop where we examine 'pairs'? Can we identify the items to move as we perform 1 pass? If we need to move it, would we know where to place it? When we move it, do we risk overwriting something we should not? Move all negative numbers to the front of the array: Before: data = [4, 8, -3, 12, -5, 6, 17, -10, 9, 1, 2, -7]. After: data = [-3, -5, -10, -7, 8, 6, 17, 4, 9, 1, 2, 12].
notes_text: This uses a leading/trailing pointer technique. Negative numbers maintain their relative order but positive numbers may be reordered.

images.description: Two array diagrams showing the before and after states. Before: mixed positive and negative values. After: all negatives moved to front. Connected by a red downward arrow.
labels: Move all negative numbers to the front of the array:

title: Task 5 - Move Negatives Trace Part 1
summary: Traces the first part of moving negatives to front using leading and trailing pointers, showing swaps when negatives are found.
main_text: Task 5. Move all negative numbers to the front of the array. Trace with leading and trailing pointers on array [4, 8, -3, 12, -5, 6, 17, -10]: leading=0, trailing=0: data[0]=4 (positive, no swap). leading=1, trailing=0: data[1]=8 (positive, no swap). leading=2, trailing=0: data[2]=-3 (negative! swap with trailing). After swap: [-3, 8, 4, ...]. leading=2, trailing=0: then swap data[leading] with data[trailing]. leading=3, trailing=1: data[3]=12 (positive). leading=4, trailing=1: data[4]=-5 (negative! swap). After swap: [-3, -5, 4, 8, ...]. leading=4, trailing=1: [-3, -5, ...then 8 swapped to position].
notes_text: The trailing pointer marks where the next negative should go. Leading pointer scans through the array. When a negative is found at leading, swap it to the trailing position.

images.description: Eight array state diagrams showing the leading and trailing pointer positions and array contents at each step, with swap arrows shown when negatives are found and moved.

title: Task 5 - Move Negatives Trace Part 2
summary: Continues the trace showing the remaining swaps and the final state of the array with all negatives at the front.
main_text: Task 5. Move all negative numbers to the front of the array. Continuing the trace: leading=5, trailing=2: data[5]=4 (in the swapped position). leading=6, trailing=2: data[6]=17 (positive). leading=7, trailing=2: data[7]=-10 (negative! swap with trailing position 2). After swap: [-3, -5, -10, ...]. The bottom section shows a second example with array [4, 8, -3, 12, -5, 6, 17, -10]: leading=8, trailing=3: final result is [-3, -5, -10, 12, 8, 6, 17, 4].
notes_text: The final array shows all negatives (-3, -5, -10) at the front in their original relative order, while positives may be reordered.

images.description: Multiple array state diagrams continuing the trace from the previous slide, showing the final swaps and resulting array state.

title: Task 5 - Move Negatives Programming Mechanics
summary: Discusses when to increment leading vs trailing pointers and states the loop invariants for the partition algorithm.
main_text: Task 5. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? When do we increment leading? When do we increment trailing? Invariants: All values behind trailing are negative. All values between leading and trailing are positive. Code template: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task ... return 0; }
notes_text: Loop invariants are a formal way to reason about correctness. Leading always increments; trailing only increments when a swap occurs.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted C++ code template for array setup.

title: Task 6 - Insert at Location Problem Statement
summary: Introduces Task 6: inserting a new value at a specific index in an array, shifting existing elements to make room.
main_text: Task 6. Assuming an array of size max, but only n occupied elements, insert a new value, v, at location, loc, shifting others back. Question: Can we do this in 1 pass or do we need a nested loop where we examine 'pairs'? Do we insert then shift? Or shift then insert? In what order should we shift the needed values? Insert 5 at location 2 into the array of 7 elements and 9 locations. Before: data = [4, 8, 7, 3, 12, 1, 9, ?, ?], n=7, max=9. After: data = [4, 8, 5, 7, 3, 12, 1, 9, ?], n=8, max=9.
notes_text: Must shift right before inserting to avoid overwriting. Shift from end toward insertion point, not the other way.

images.description: Two array diagrams showing before and after insertion of value 5 at index 2, with a red downward arrow between them. Variables n and max shown beside the arrays.

title: Task 6 - Wrong Way to Shift (Left to Right)
summary: Shows why shifting from left to right (low index to high) is incorrect - it overwrites values before they can be moved.
main_text: Task 6. Insert 5 at location 2 into the array of 7 elements and 9 locations. Wrong approach - shifting left to right: k=2: data[k+1] = data[k] copies 7 to position 3, but overwrites 3. k=3: data[k+1] = data[k] copies 7 (the already-copied value) to position 4. k=4: copies 7 again. Result: [4, 8, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, ?, ?] - all positions from 2 onward become 7. A prohibition symbol indicates this approach is wrong.
notes_text: This demonstrates the classic pitfall of shifting in the wrong direction. Each shift overwrites the next element before it can be saved.

images.description: Four array state diagrams showing the incorrect left-to-right shift, with data[k+1]=data[k] labels on the right. The value 7 propagates through all positions. A red prohibition symbol at the bottom indicates this is wrong.

title: Task 6 - Correct Way to Shift (Right to Left)
summary: Shows the correct approach to shifting elements from right to left (high index to low) before inserting.
main_text: Task 6. Insert 5 at location 2 into the array of 7 elements and 9 locations. Correct approach - shifting right to left: k=6: data[k+1] = data[k] copies 9 to position 7. k=5: data[k+1] = data[k] copies 1 to position 6. k=4: copies 12 to position 5. k=3: copies 3 to position 4. k=2: copies 7 to position 3. Now position 2 is free to insert the new value. Each step shows data[k+1] = data[k] on the right side.
notes_text: By starting from the rightmost element and working left, each element is safely moved to the right before its position is needed.

images.description: Five array state diagrams showing the correct right-to-left shift operation, with each step copying one element one position to the right, starting from the end.

title: Task 6 - Final Insertion Step
summary: Shows the final step of inserting the value 5 at the now-empty location 2 and incrementing n.
main_text: Task 6. Insert 5 at location 2 into the array of 7 elements and 9 locations. After shifting is complete, position 2 is available: data[loc] = val; assigns 5 to index 2. n++; increments the element count from 7 to 8. Final result: data = [4, 8, 5, 7, 3, 12, 1, 9, ?], n=8, max=9.
notes_text: The insertion is a two-phase process: first shift elements right to make room, then place the new value and update n.

images.description: Two array state diagrams showing the state just before and after inserting value 5 at index 2, with data[loc]=val and n++ annotations.

title: Task 6 - Insertion Programming Mechanics
summary: Discusses implementation questions for array insertion: shift direction (k to k+1 vs k-1 to k) and loop start/stop positions.
main_text: Task 6. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Do we want to move from k to k+1 OR k-1 to k? Based on the above where should we start and stop our loop? Code template: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task ... return 0; }
notes_text: The loop should start at k=n-1 and go down to k=loc, using data[k+1]=data[k]. Then insert data[loc]=val and increment n.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted C++ code template for array setup.

title: Task 7 - Find Unique Number Problem Statement
summary: Introduces Task 7: finding the one number in an array that has no duplicate pair, using nested loop comparison.
main_text: Task 7. Given there is 1 number that does NOT have a duplicate (pair), find and output that unique number. Questions: Is this generating all pairs again? Might we be able to answer 'early'? Find the unique number: Array data = [4, 7, 4, 12, 7, 3, 12] with empty gray cells below. Sample Data: 33 13 23 72 20 6 61 66 46 54 33 1 17 47 29 73 18 1 50 73 89 46 5 98 13 32 70 32 10 10 87 53 99 12 5 61 12 18 76 96 87 60 96 82 47 52 29 76 93 70 71 6 7 39 48 48 17 99 36 82 72 60 71 89 36 98 54 93 7 66 39 52 53 50 20
notes_text: Every number appears exactly twice except for one unique number. The approach requires checking each element against all others.

images.description: Array diagram showing data=[4,7,4,12,7,3,12] and a large sample dataset in a box below.

title: Task 7 - Finding Unique with One-Way Pairs (Fails)
summary: Shows that checking only one ordering of pairs (j,k where k>j) fails to correctly identify the unique number because the match for the second occurrence is missed.
main_text: Task 7. Find the unique number finding all pairs (with only one ordering rather than both for each pair). Array: [8, 3, 5, 6, 8, 3, 5]. Trace: J=0, K=1 through K=6: checking 8 against all others, finds match at K=4 (8). J=1, K=2 through K=6: checking 3, finds match at K=5 (3). J=2, K=3 through K=6: checking 5, finds match at K=6 (5). But for J=2, K=6 with value 3 - we didn't find a match for the 2nd item in a pair that DID exist! The problem: when we find a pair (3,3) at J=1,K=5, the second 3 at index 5 is never checked as a 'first' element against later elements.
notes_text: This approach of only checking (j,k) where k>j fails because the second occurrence of a paired number might appear to be unique when checked as j.

images.description: Array trace diagrams in two columns showing J and K positions with highlighted matching pairs. A prohibition symbol and note at bottom indicates the approach fails.

title: Task 7 - Finding Unique with Both Orderings
summary: Shows the correct approach using all pairs in both orderings (k starts at 0, not j+1), checking each element against every other element.
main_text: Task 7. Find the unique number with all pairs (in both orders). Array: [8, 3, 5, 6, 8, 3, 5]. Trace for J=0: K=0 (skip self), K=1: 8 vs 3, K=2: 8 vs 5, K=3: 8 vs 6, K=4: 8 vs 8 (match found! 8 has a pair). J=1: K=0: 3 vs 8, K=1 (skip self), K=2: 3 vs 5, K=3: 3 vs 6, K=4: 3 vs 8, K=5: 3 vs 3 (match found!). For J=2: checking element 8 at index 0, finds match at K=4. And so on for each element.
notes_text: By letting K range from 0 to n (skipping when k==j), each element is fully checked against all others. This correctly identifies unmatched elements.

images.description: Array trace diagrams in two columns showing J and K positions, checking both orderings. Green/yellow highlighted cells show matches found.

title: Task 7 - Complete Trace Finding 6 as Unique
summary: Complete trace showing all elements being checked, concluding that 6 is the unique number because it has no match in the array.
main_text: Task 7. Find the unique number. Array: [8, 3, 5, 6, 8, 3, 5]. Continuing the trace for later J values: J=3: checking 8 at index 0 vs 5 at index 2, then 5 vs 6, 3 vs 6, 5 vs 6, etc. J=4: K=0 through K=6 checking element 6 against all others. 6 vs 8, 6 vs 3, 6 vs 5, 6 vs 6... but wait, there is no other 6 in the array! title: Sequential vs. Random Access
summary: Explains the two main array access patterns: sequential access (looping through all elements) and random access (computing a specific index directly).
main_text: Sequential vs. Random Access. Most array-based tasks fall into either a sequential-access pattern or random-access pattern. Sequential access iterates (loops) through all elements. Used for tasks that require looking at all elements in the worst case. Random access computes the ONE index to access. Used for tasks that only require accessing one specific element. Sequential example: int total = 0; for(int i=0; i < 20; i++){ total += scores[i]; } Array scores at addresses 520-1076 with indices [0]-[19] containing values 96, 84, 93, ..., 90. Random access example: int stuID; cout << 'Enter ID\n'; cin >> stuID; cout << 'Your score: '; cout << scores[stuID]; cout << endl; A stuID value of 2 directly accesses scores[2]=93.
notes_text: Sequential access is O(n) while random access is O(1). Many array algorithms combine both patterns.

images.description: Two diagrams: Left shows sequential access with an arrow sweeping across all array elements with a loop summing them. Right shows random access where stuID=2 directly indexes into scores[2]=93.

title: Arrays as Look-Up Tables
summary: Explains how to use one array's values as indices into another array, creating a look-up table pattern for precomputed results.
main_text: Arrays as Look-Up Tables. Use the value of one array as the index of another. Suppose you are given some integers as data [in the range of 0 to 5]. Suppose computing squares of integers was difficult (no built-in function for it). Could compute them yourself, record answer in another array and use data to 'look-up' the square. Code example 1 (two-step): // the data int data[8] = {3, 2, 0, 5, 1, 4, 5, 3}; // The LUT int squares[6] = {0,1,4,9,16,25}; for(int i=0; i < 8; i++){ int x = data[i]; int x_sq = squares[x]; cout << i << ',' << x_sq << endl; } Code example 2 (combined): for(int i=0; i < 8; i++){ int x_sq = squares[data[i]]; cout << i << ',' << x_sq << endl; }
notes_text: The LUT pattern is a form of random access. The value from data[] is used as an index into squares[], avoiding recomputation. This is a common optimization technique.

In this program the values of the priority array can be used to check the requests array in order from most to least priority. Example trace with pri=[0,1,2,3] and req=[0,1,0,1]: Selected=1 (pri[1]=1 is highest priority requestor). pri updates to [0,2,3,1]. req=[0,1,1,1]: Selected=2. pri=[0,3,1,2]. req=[0,0,1,0]: Selected=2. pri=[0,3,1,2]. req=[1,1,1,1]: Selected=0. pri=[3,1,2,0]. req=[1,1,1,1]: Selected=3. pri=[1,2,0,3]. req=[0,0,0,0]: Quit.
notes_text: The priority array acts as a look-up table that determines the order in which requestors are checked. After each selection, priorities are updated.

Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task for(int j=0; j < n; j++) { for(int k=j+1; k < n; k++) { cout << data[j] << ',' << data[k] << ' '; } } cout << endl; return 0; }

main_text: Task 3 - Solution. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Are the indexes independent or is one dependent on another? How and when are we ready to print our answer? How do we stop (one or both loops)? Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task bool allUnique = true; for(int j=0; j < n; j++) { for(int k=j+1; k < n; k++) { if(data[j] == data[k]){ allUnique = false; break; } } if(!allUnique) break; } if(allUnique) { cout << 'All unique' << endl; } else { cout << 'Not all unique' << endl; } return 0; }

title: Task 5 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for moving negatives to front using leading/trailing pointer technique with single-pass swap.
main_text: Task 5 - Solution. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? When do we increment leading? When do we increment trailing? Invariants: All values behind trailing are negative. All values between leading and trailing are positive. Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int lead, trail = 0; for(lead=0; lead < n; lead++) { if(data[lead] < 0) { // swap leading and trailing int temp = data[lead]; data[lead] = data[trail]; data[trail] = temp; // only increment if we move trail++; } } return 0; }
notes_text: Leading always advances (via for loop). Trailing only advances when a negative is found and swapped. The invariants guarantee correctness.

title: Task 6 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for inserting a value at a specific location with bounds checking, right-to-left shift, and n increment.
main_text: Task 6 - Solution. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Do we want to move from k to k+1 OR k-1 to k? Based on the above where should we start and stop our loop? Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[20]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int loc, val; cin >> loc >> val; if(n < 20 && loc >= 0 && loc <= n){ for(int k=n-1; k >= loc; k--) { data[k+1] = data[k]; } data[loc] = val; n++; } else { cout << 'Invalid' << endl; } cout << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: Bounds checking ensures n < max (20) and loc is valid. The loop goes from n-1 down to loc, shifting each element right. Then insert and increment n.

title: Task 7 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for finding the unique number using nested loops with j!=k check and boolean unique flag.
main_text: Task 7 - Solution. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? How do we avoid matching ourself? How do we know we've found a unique item? When and how can we stop early? Variations: Allow 0 or more unique values and output the unique values OR output 'All have a pair' if each number has a pair. Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, val, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task for(int j=0; j < n; j++) { bool unique = true; for(int k=0; k < n; k++) { if(j != k){ if(data[j] == data[k]){ unique = false; break; } } } if(unique){ cout << data[j] << endl; break; } } return 0; }
notes_text: The if(j != k) check prevents self-comparison. The inner break exits when a match is found. The outer break exits when the unique element is identified.

title: Task 8 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for merging two sorted arrays using three while loops for the three phases of merge.
main_text: Task 8 - Sol. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? What cases or 'phases' exist for the merge process? What two elements should be compared and what element should be placed in the output? Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n1=0, n2=0, in1[20], in2[20], out[40]; int num; // Read array 1 cin >> num; while(num != -1){ in1[n1++] = num; cin >> num; } // Read array 2 cin >> num; while(num != -1){ in2[n2++] = num; cin >> num; } // now perform the given task int r1 = 0, r2 = 0, w = 0; while(r1 < n1 && r2 < n2) { if(in1[r1] < in2[r2]) { out[w++] = in1[r1++]; } else { out[w++] = in2[r2++]; } } while(r1 < n1) { // place remaining in1 out[w++] = in1[r1++]; } while(r2 < n2) { // place remaining in2 out[w++] = in2[r2++]; } // Output the results return 0; }
notes_text: Three phases: (1) compare and place smaller while both arrays have elements, (2) copy remaining from in1, (3) copy remaining from in2. Uses post-increment on indices.

title: Task 9 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for inserting into a sorted array using while loop to find location, then for loop to shift, with capacity check.
main_text: Task 9 - Sol. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Are the indexes independent or is one dependent on another? How and when are we ready to print our answer? How do we stop (one or both loops)? Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int val, loc = -1, curr = 0; cin >> val; if(n < 100){ while(curr < n && val > data[curr] ) { curr++; } loc = curr; for(int curr = n-1; curr >= loc; curr--) { data[curr+1] = data[curr]; } data[loc] = val; n++; } else { cout << 'No room' << endl; } // Output the results return 0; }
notes_text: Two sequential operations: (1) while loop to find insertion location by scanning until data[curr] >= val, (2) for loop to shift right from n-1 down to loc. Then insert and increment n.

title: Task 10 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for removing the first occurrence of a value: find with break, then shift left, then decrement n.
main_text: Task 10 - Sol. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? In what order should you shift? Will you shift from k to k-1 or k+1 to k? And where would you stop? Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int val, loc; cin >> val; // find first occurrence of val for(loc = 0; loc < n; loc++) { if(data[loc] == val) { break; } } if(loc < n) { // shift items up from loc to n // invariant: data[loc] is always safe to overwrite for( ; loc < n-1; loc++) { data[loc] = data[loc+1]; } n--; } // Output the results ... return 0; }
notes_text: The find loop uses break when found. If loc < n after the loop, the value was found and we shift left. The invariant notes that data[loc] is always safe to overwrite.

title: Task 11 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for removing all occurrences using leading/trailing pointer single-pass technique.
main_text: Task 11 - Sol. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Do we just need to track the maximum VALUE or the INDEX of the maximum value? Given that you can move the maximum number to the end of the array, how could this be used to SORT the entire array? Repeat the process for the first n-1 elements, then repeat for the first n-2 elements, etc. Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int val, lead, trail; cin >> val; trail = 0; for(lead = 0; lead < n; lead++) { if(data[lead] != val) { data[trail] = data[lead]; trail++; } } n = trail; // Output the results for(int i=0; i < n; i++){ cout << data[i] << ' '; } cout << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: When data[lead] != val, copy to trail position and advance trail. When equal to val, only advance lead (skip). n = trail gives the new size.

title: Task 12a - Selection Sort Step Solution
summary: Complete C++ solution for finding the max and swapping it to the end using index tracking (selection sort step).
main_text: Task 12a - Sol. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Do we just need to track the maximum VALUE or the INDEX of the maximum value? Given that you can move the maximum number to the end of the array, how could this be used to SORT the entire array? Repeat the process for the first n-1 elements, then repeat for the first n-2 elements, etc. Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, val, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int cmax = 0; for(int i=1; i < n; i++) { if(data[i] > data[cmax]){ cmax = i; } } // swap the max and end element int temp = data[n-1]; data[n-1] = data[cmax]; data[cmax] = temp; // Print out results for(int i=0; i < n; i++){ cout << data[i] << ' '; } cout << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: cmax starts at 0 and updates whenever a larger element is found. After the loop, one swap places the max at the end. This is one step of selection sort.
